summary: Presents a framework to help writers of certificate policies and certification practice statements for public key infrastructures. It provides a comprehensive list of topics that might need covering. It obsoletes RFC 2527 and is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC helps organizations write documents explaining how they issue and manage certificates. It distinguishes shared requirements from the detailed practices of an individual certification authority.

questions: what is a certification practice statement
what is the difference between a cp and cps
subtitle: A framework of topics for certificate policies and certification practice statements.

tldr.problem: People relying on certificates need information about the rules and practices behind their issuance and management.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC distinguishes certificate policies from certification practice statements and provides a flexible list of topics writers can address.
tldr.outcome: It is a framework, not a particular policy or legal advice, and it obsoletes RFC 2527.

today: RFC 3647 is an Informational framework published in November 2003. It obsoletes RFC 2527; the unit metadata lists no RFC that later obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
A public-key certificate binds a public key to information about a person, organization, device, or other subject. A relying party’s trust in that binding depends in part on how the certification authority operates, protects its systems, and handles certificate responsibilities.

This RFC explains certificate policies and certification practice statements and offers a framework for drafting them. It does not define a specific policy, prescribe particular practices, or provide legal advice. The framework is intended as a flexible tool, not a rigid formula.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate is useful only if its reader can assess how it was issued and managed. This framework helps organizations describe those practices without prescribing one set of rules.

sections.title: Policy and Practice Statement
sections.content:
A certificate policy (CP) states requirements for a community or class of applications with shared security needs. It commonly applies across multiple certification authorities and can support interoperability. A certification practice statement (CPS) describes how a particular authority or organization carries out its work and meets applicable requirements.

A CPS is generally more detailed than a CP. One certification authority may support several CPs, and several authorities with different practices may support the same CP. Neither document automatically creates a contract; an agreement may incorporate its terms.
sections.plainLanguage: A policy states the rules participants are expected to meet. A practice statement describes how one certification authority follows those rules.

sections.title: Policy Information in Certificates
sections.content:
X.509 version 3 certificates can include a Certificate Policies extension that identifies applicable policies. A relying party can use those identifiers when deciding whether a certificate is appropriate for a purpose. When a policy indication is marked critical, use of the certificate is restricted to the listed policies.

Other extensions support policy mappings between certification authorities and constraints on policy processing. Policy qualifiers can point to a CPS or provide a user notice. These fields connect certificate processing with the policy information described in the documents.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate can identify the policy that applies to it. Other certificate fields can connect policies across authorities or restrict which policies are accepted.

sections.title: Topics in a Set of Provisions
sections.content:
The framework organizes a CP or CPS as a set of provisions covering standard topics. Its nine primary components include introduction; publication and repository; identification and authentication; certificate life-cycle operations; facility, management, and operational controls; technical security controls; certificate, CRL, and OCSP profiles; compliance audit; and business and legal matters.

Writers can address topics such as identity checks, certificate issuance and revocation, key protection, records, audits, fees, warranties, and liability. A document may state that a topic has no stipulation, and writers may add more detailed subsections.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework offers nine main areas to consider, from proving identities to protecting keys and describing legal terms. Writers can say when a topic has no rule rather than inventing one.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 2527
sections.content:
RFC 3647 revises the framework in RFC 2527 based on experience with certificate policies and practice statements. It reorganizes the material and adds or expands topics including certificate life-cycle procedures, key escrow and recovery, OCSP, audit, and business and legal matters.

The framework retains its role as an aid for document writers. It does not decide what a particular authority must promise or how a particular legal issue should be handled.
sections.plainLanguage: This edition reorganizes and expands an earlier checklist. It still leaves each organization to decide which provisions fit its own policy and practices.
